tasks.short: Review medication history, choose a psychotropic drug and dose with the patient, prescribe, and inform the general practitioner.

steps.what: Nurse specialist gathers the medication history from the record and by calling the pharmacy
Nurse specialist chooses the psychotropic drug and dose together with the patient
Nurse specialist types the prescriptions field by field in the record
Nurse specialist resolves interaction and contraindication alerts on the draft
Nurse specialist signs the prescription
Nurse specialist sends the prescription to the patient's pharmacy
Pharmacist checks the prescription and dispenses the medication
Nurse specialist writes a medication letter for the general practitioner
Nurse specialist sends the medication letter to the general practitioner

tasks.design: The electronic health record ({OTHER}) imports the dispensed-medication overview from the national exchange when the patient has consented, and offers favourite regimens for common psychotropic starts and switches. The national drug database keeps checking interactions and doses as today, and a medication letter to the general practitioner is generated from the signed prescription with one line of rationale typed by the nurse specialist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Medication histories were pieced together by phone, and letters to the general practitioner were typed for every change.
tasks.enabler_now: Records exchange medication data with consent, and letter templates fill from prescription fields.
tasks.still_hard: Choosing the drug is clinical judgement shared with the patient; only a named practitioner may prescribe.
tasks.human_edge: Weighing side effects against what the patient can live with and earning their trust in the treatment.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in prescribing rights; less phoning and typing around each prescription.

reach.task: Reconcile psychotropic medication at first dispensing
reach.learn: Whether the shared overview cuts their callbacks to prescribers.

evidence.claim: The national drug database checks interactions, contraindications, doses and duplicates, with content set by the pharmacists' association.
A prescription comes from a named practitioner under national rules; software drafts, it does not prescribe.
Exchanging medication data between care providers needs the patient's consent under national rules.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from gathering the medication history to the general practitioner informed; dispensing is outside.

Input contract: dispensing data from community pharmacies through the national exchange, with the patient's consent recorded at intake; favourite regimens set by the nurse specialists with the hospital pharmacist; fallback is calling the pharmacy.
Interaction checking already runs in the record; that runtime earns no saving.
Pharmacist time is outside the nurse specialist's savings.
unknowns: Share of patients who consent to data exchange.
How often prescriptions change per patient per year.
research_questions: How much time does a medication history take with and without the exchange?

already_counted.description: Nurse specialist checks the imported overview against what the patient says they take.
Nurse specialist checks the generated letter before signing.

incremental.description: Nurse specialist keeps favourite regimens current.
Hospital pharmacist reviews the favourites list each year.

approvals.approved_version: The prescription as signed by the nurse specialist in s5; a change needs a new signature.
The medication letter as written and checked by the nurse specialist in s7.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Patients who refuse data exchange still need the phone history, and complex switches need letters written by hand.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Follow up medication use, side effects, blood levels and refills, judge the effect and adjust the treatment plan.

steps.what: Nurse specialist asks the patient about medication use, side effects and effect
Patient fills in the side-effect rating scale on paper in the clinic
Nurse specialist hands out a side-effect rating scale on paper and scores it
Nurse specialist works out which blood levels and metabolic checks are due and orders them
Nurse specialist searches earlier levels, weight and blood pressure in the record
Nurse specialist phones the pharmacy to check refills and adherence
Nurse specialist judges the results of the medication and adjusts the treatment plan
Nurse specialist writes the follow-up note with scores and levels in the record

tasks.design: The patient fills in the side-effect scale in the portal of the electronic health record ({OTHER}) before the visit and it is scored automatically. A monitoring schedule per drug (lithium levels, metabolic checks for antipsychotics) builds a due list for the nurse specialist to confirm before orders go, a trend view shows levels, weight and refills together, and the follow-up note pre-fills scores and values.
tasks.previous_blocker: Monitoring depended on the clinician remembering what was due, and refill data meant a phone call.
tasks.enabler_now: Records support patient questionnaires, scheduled orders, trend views and medication data exchange as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Judging whether a drug works needs the conversation; patients may not fill in scales before visits.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing what the patient does not say about side effects and adjusting treatment with them.

ambition.what: Every patient on lithium or antipsychotics checked on schedule, not only those whose clinician remembers.

tasks.altitude: The nurse specialist confirms due lists and reads one view; treatment decisions stay theirs.

reach.task: Continue metabolic monitoring after discharge to primary care
reach.learn: Whether the monitoring schedule can travel with the patient.

evidence.claim: Records can run monitoring schedules per drug, patient questionnaires and trend views as configuration.
The inspectorate names medication errors from wrong registration as a risk providers must manage.
Solely automated decisions with significant effect need a specific legal basis; the nurse specialist confirms every order.

assumptions: Boundary: from the follow-up visit to the updated treatment plan; prescribing changes are a separate task.

Input contract: side-effect scale completed by the patient in the portal before the visit (fallback paper in the waiting room); monitoring schedule per drug kept by the hospital pharmacist from the guideline; refill data from the national exchange with consent.
Patients already fill in the scale on paper; filling it in the portal takes about the same time, priced as customer time.
The conversation and clinical judgement do not change.
unknowns: Share of patients who use the portal.
research_questions: Does the due list raise the share of patients monitored on time?

already_counted.description: Nurse specialist reviews portal scores flagged above threshold.
Nurse specialist confirms or edits the due list before orders go.

incremental.description: Nurse specialist reminds patients who skip portal questionnaires.
Hospital pharmacist keeps monitoring schedules current.

approvals.approved_version: Due-list orders as confirmed by the nurse specialist; added tests need a new confirmation.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Patients who do not use the portal or consent to exchange keep paper scales and pharmacy calls.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Prepare from referral and records, interview and observe the patient, discuss in the team and write the assessment.

steps.what: Nurse specialist reads the referral and earlier treatment records before the intake

loop.input: The referral letter and earlier treatment notes, discharge letters and medication lists in the record.
loop.output: A one-page history with earlier diagnoses, treatments tried, medication and risk events, each line linked to its source.
loop.check: Every line must cite a document; diagnoses and medication must match coded record fields; risk events from the incident register must all appear, else the summary is marked incomplete.
loop.stop: One draft and one retry; then the nurse specialist reads the records.
loop.why_not_simpler: Earlier treatment is described in free-text letters by different clinicians; coded fields miss what was tried and why it stopped.

steps.what: Nurse specialist interviews patients and family and evaluates behavior during the session
Nurse specialist discusses working diagnoses in the multidisciplinary team
Psychiatrist confirms the diagnosis and treatment advice
Nurse specialist writes the assessment report from session notes
Nurse specialist sends the assessment letter to the referring general practitioner

tasks.design: Before intake a bounded step drafts a one-page history from the referral and earlier records in the electronic health record ({OTHER}), each line linked to its source. With the patient's consent the session is recorded and a draft assessment report is produced for the nurse specialist to validate; once signed, the letter goes to the referring general practitioner through secure care messaging.
tasks.previous_blocker: Earlier records were read in full before each intake, and reports were typed after the session.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch scribes record consultations for clinicians to validate, and record tools answer questions on the record.
tasks.still_hard: Many patients in mental health decline recording; drafts can miss nuance, and the inspectorate expects testing and monitoring.
tasks.human_edge: Building trust in the first meeting and reading behaviour that no transcript holds.
tasks.altitude: The nurse specialist validates drafts instead of writing from scratch; diagnosis stays with them and the psychiatrist.

reach.learn: Whether consent rates and draft quality differ between professions.

evidence.claim: A Dutch scribe records the consultation, the clinician validates, and the note goes into the record.
A Dutch tool answers clinicians' questions on the record; its MDR certification is in progress.
Across 236,153 scribe notes, self-estimated time per note fell from 6.69 to 4.72 minutes; three of seven authors were from the vendor.
Ambient recording captures staff performance, so the works council must consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from preparing the intake to the assessment letter sent; treatment is outside.

Input contract: referral letters from general practitioners through secure messaging; incident register kept by the quality officer; recording consent asked and stored by the nurse specialist at the start of the session; fallback is reading records and typing notes.
Psychiatrist time is outside the nurse specialist's savings.
Interview and team discussion do not change.
s5 is part of documenting assessment results, which sibling task 29-1141.02:17329 covers; its saving is counted there, so s5 keeps its full time here.
unknowns: Share of patients who consent to recording.
Length of earlier records per patient.
research_questions: Do drafted histories miss risk events that the full record shows?

already_counted.description: Nurse specialist checks the drafted history against sources.
Nurse specialist validates the drafted report and quoted risk statements.

incremental.description: Nurse specialist asks recording consent and handles refusals.
Clinical informatics audits samples and monitors after updates.

approvals.approved_version: The assessment report as validated and signed by the nurse specialist in s5; any change needs a new signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Where most patients decline recording, only the history summary and letter sending save time.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check for somatic causes of psychiatric symptoms: history, examination, lab tests and general practitioner data, then diagnose or refer.

steps.what: Nurse specialist takes the somatic history, substance use and medication
Nurse specialist does a physical examination and measures vital signs
Nurse specialist picks screening lab tests one by one to rule out physical disorders
Nurse specialist requests results and history from the general practitioner by phone and letter
Nurse specialist weighs physiologically- and psychologically-based explanations and decides
General practitioner or internist assesses the suspected somatic cause on referral
Nurse specialist records the diagnosis and its classification code in the record

tasks.design: Configure a fixed somatic screening order set in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) for new presentations such as first psychosis or late-onset depression, and retrieve the general practitioner's summary and recent results through the national exchange when the patient consents. A searchable classification picklist replaces free coding; the weighing of explanations stays with the nurse specialist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Somatic data sat with the general practitioner and arrived by phone or letter days later.
tasks.enabler_now: Records exchange general practitioner summaries with consent and support order sets as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Telling somatic from psychiatric causes is clinical judgement; data from other providers is often incomplete.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing that the confusion looks medical, not psychiatric, and sending the patient on quickly.

ambition.what: Somatic screening done for every new patient before a psychiatric diagnosis is recorded.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in diagnostic rights; data arrives before the decision instead of after.

reach.task: Share somatic data when referring to mental health care
reach.learn: Which data mental health teams actually use from the summary.

evidence.claim: Records can retrieve general practitioner summaries through a national exchange when the patient consents.
Health data is special category data; solely automated care decisions need an explicit legal basis.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from the somatic history to the coded diagnosis or referral; treatment is outside.

Input contract: general practitioner summary through the national exchange with consent recorded at intake; order set content set by the psychiatry and internal medicine leads; screening lab results returned by the lab to the record; classification list in the record; fallback is phoning the practice.
General practitioner and lab time is outside the nurse specialist's savings.
History, examination and the decision do not change.
unknowns: Share of patients who consent to the exchange.
How often a somatic cause is found today.
research_questions: Does a fixed screening set find more somatic causes than case-by-case ordering?

already_counted.description: Nurse specialist reviews the retrieved summary for gaps and asks for what is missing.

incremental.description: Nurse specialist records exchange consent and handles failed retrievals.
Clinical leads keep the screening order set current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Patients without a general practitioner on the exchange, or who refuse consent, keep the phone and letter route.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The nurse specialist keeps the conversations, examinations and decisions; histories, monitoring lists, letters and reports become drafts to check.
skills_to_grow: Validating drafted histories and reports critically
Asking for recording and data-exchange consent well
Working from due lists and trend views
role.ambitious_version: A nurse specialist who sees every patient's medication, monitoring and somatic data before the visit, and spends the visit on the patient.
